opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's been a really interesting journey, and in some ways it's a story about taking an idea that worked spectacularly well in one domain and asking whether the assumptions everyone made about the other domain were actually necessary.

If you go back to the early days, a lot of the work my group did was on score-based models: learning the gradient of the log density, then using that to gradually turn noise into data. That framework turned out to be incredibly powerful for continuous data like images, audio, and video. The key insight was that instead of generating something one piece at a time, you start with a rough, noisy version of the whole object and refine it in parallel over a number of steps. You get coarse-to-fine generation, you can trade compute for quality, and you have a lot of control.

Text was always the obvious holdout. Language is discrete, it's tokens, and there's no natural notion of adding a little bit of Gaussian noise to a word. So the field largely concluded that autoregressive models, predicting the next token left to right, were simply the right tool for language, and diffusion was for pixels.

What we found is that you can define a diffusion process directly on discrete spaces. Instead of adding Gaussian noise, you corrupt tokens, for example by masking them or replacing them, and then you learn to reverse that corruption. The technical challenge was that the score, which was so central in the continuous case, isn't defined for discrete data. So we introduced the idea of learning ratios of probabilities between neighboring sequences, what we called concrete scores, and trained them with a score-entropy objective. That gave us a principled discrete analogue, and for the first time diffusion language models started to match autoregressive models of similar size on perplexity, which a lot of people didn't think was possible.

Once you have that, the benefits from images carry over. You're no longer bottlenecked by generating one token at a time, so you can generate many tokens in parallel and get dramatically faster inference on the same hardware. You also get a model that can revise earlier parts of its output rather than being locked into whatever it committed to, which matters for reasoning and for controllability.

Code turned out to be a particularly natural fit. Code isn't really written strictly left to right; programmers jump around, fill in a function body, fix a signature, go back and change a variable name. Infilling and editing are first-class operations for a diffusion model, and the speed matters a lot in coding assistants, where latency directly affects whether the tool feels useful. That's a big part of why we started Inception, to take these diffusion LLMs out of the lab and show they can be both high quality and much faster in real products.

So the path, in a sentence, was: take the coarse-to-fine, parallel refinement idea that made image generation work, figure out the right mathematics to make it work on discrete tokens, and then realize that for text and especially code, the properties you get, speed, editing, and global coherence, are exactly what those applications need.

r001.rationale: The response explains that text is discrete and describes adapting diffusion by corrupting tokens and learning to reverse that process, then applies the approach to code.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. The way I usually tell it is that the path was really about questioning an assumption that most people had baked in so deeply they didn't even notice it was there.

So the diffusion story on the image side is fairly well known by now. Back around 2019, 2020 in my group at Stanford, Yang Song and I were working on score-based generative models, and Jonathan Ho and his collaborators were working on DDPMs, and those two threads converged into what we now call diffusion models. The core idea is that instead of generating a sample in one shot, or one piece at a time, you start from pure noise and iteratively refine it. Every step, the model looks at the whole canvas and makes a small global improvement. And that turned out to be an incredibly good fit for images, because an image is inherently a parallel object. There's no natural reason the top-left pixel should come before the bottom-right one.

Text was a completely different world. The whole field had basically converged on autoregression, left to right, one token at a time, and it works remarkably well. The transformer plus next-token prediction is a very good recipe. But if you step back, there's something a bit strange about it. When you or I write a paragraph, or write a function, we don't commit to each word irrevocably and never look back. We sketch, we restructure, we fix the beginning after we've seen how the end turned out. Autoregressive models structurally can't do that. And they have a very practical cost too, which is that generation is serial. You can't produce token one hundred until you've produced token ninety-nine. So you're fundamentally latency-bound and you can't use the hardware well.

The natural question for us was, can we bring the diffusion paradigm over? Can we treat a sequence of text the way we treat an image, start from a fully noised or fully masked sequence, and iteratively denoise the whole thing in parallel? And the honest answer for a long time was, it's hard. The reason is that text is discrete. In image space you can add a little bit of Gaussian noise to a pixel, and the math of score matching and stochastic differential equations works beautifully. There's no such thing as adding a little bit of noise to the word "the." So the first few years were really about building the right mathematical machinery for discrete diffusion. There was early work on continuous relaxations, embedding tokens into a continuous space and diffusing there, which was interesting but tended to lag behind in quality. And then there was the discrete route, things like masking and unmasking tokens, or defining corruption processes directly over the vocabulary. In my group, Aaron Lou and Chenlin Meng and others worked on what we called score entropy discrete diffusion, which was really about figuring out what the analog of the score function is when your state space is discrete, and getting a principled training objective out of it. That was the moment, for me, where it felt like the gap to autoregressive models at small scale had closed enough that this was no longer a curiosity.

The second half of the path is the engineering and scaling half, and that's a lot of what we've been doing at Inception. Having a nice objective on a small benchmark is one thing. Showing that this works at the scale where people actually care, and that the parallel generation translates into real wall-clock speedups on real GPUs, is another. The payoff we were betting on was that if you can refine a whole block of tokens at once, you can be dramatically faster, and you also get a kind of built-in ability to edit and fix. And code was the obvious first place to prove it. Code is highly structured, correctness matters, latency matters a lot in interactive settings like an IDE, and the ability to go back and fix an earlier line after you've written the later ones is actually what a programmer does. So code wasn't a detour from language, it was the sharpest test of the thesis.

So if I compress it: images taught us that iterative, parallel refinement is a powerful way to generate, text forced us to reinvent that idea for discrete data, and code was where the practical advantages, speed and controllability, became undeniable enough that we felt it was worth building a company around.

r001.rationale: The response explains that extending diffusion from images to text required adapting the method to discrete data, including masking or unmasking tokens and corruption processes over the vocabulary.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that diffusion gives us a general recipe for generation. You start with data, gradually corrupt it, and then train a model to reverse that corruption. For images, adding Gaussian noise is a very natural choice because pixel values are continuous. And we’ve seen how powerful that approach can be.

With text and code, the question is: what does corruption mean for something discrete? You can’t necessarily add a small amount of noise to a word and get another meaningful word. But you can mask tokens, for example, and train a model to recover what was there. That gives you a similar process: start with a heavily corrupted sequence and progressively fill in or refine it.

What’s exciting is that this offers a different generation strategy from producing one token at a time, left to right. You can potentially generate many tokens in parallel, and use context from both directions. For code, that’s particularly appealing because different parts of a program have to agree with one another.

Of course, parallel generation doesn’t automatically mean faster generation—you still have to account for the number of refinement steps. So the challenge is to get the quality, the speed, and the consistency together. The underlying diffusion idea carries over, but the representation and the corruption process need to fit the structure of language.

r001.rationale: The response explains that text and code are discrete, so diffusion must use a corruption process suited to them, such as masking tokens and recovering them.

sol-6.1.text:
The key idea is to learn how to reverse a corruption process. For images, you can gradually add noise to the pixels and train a model to recover the original image. Once you learn that process, you can start from noise and generate a new image by repeatedly refining it.

With text and code, the challenge is that the data is discrete. Adding a little Gaussian noise to a token doesn’t have the same natural interpretation as adding noise to a pixel. So you need to rethink the corruption process—for example, by masking tokens—and learn how to reverse it.

What’s exciting is that this gives you a different way to generate sequences. Instead of committing to one token at a time, from left to right, you can work on multiple positions and refine the sequence over several steps. For code, that’s an appealing possibility because choices in one part of a program can depend on things elsewhere. The question is how to turn that flexibility into good quality and efficient generation.

r001.rationale: The response says text and code are discrete data and explains adapting diffusion via token masking and reverse corruption to generate sequences.
